sections.title: Sunday Pancakes — Opening Passage (Private Draft)
sections.body:
The one thing I know for certain is this: Sunday mornings belonged to pancakes, and pancakes belonged to Aunt. Everything after that first certainty is mine to build slowly, one remembered detail at a time, without filling the gaps with things I cannot honestly claim.

So I begin where the ground is firm. The griddle, warm before the house was fully awake. The smell that traveled ahead of any invitation, calling me from whatever room I slept in. Aunt at the counter, quiet and steady, doing something ordinary that somehow made the whole week stand up straight.

What I cannot confirm, I will not pretend to know. I do not remember the color of the kitchen walls, or the exact words she said when the first pancake came off the griddle. I do not remember whether it was summer or winter, whether anyone else sat at the table, or how old I was. Those things are open — not lost, but waiting for the moment a real detail returns and answers them.

Here is what the memory gives me without asking anything back: the certainty of being expected. The ritual of a Sunday that repeated itself gently. The knowledge that Aunt was there, and that pancakes were the way she said so.

For now, that is the scene. Three sentences of it are true in a way I can defend. The rest — the exact temperature of the room, the shape of the plate, the sound of the syrup — I am marking plainly as imagination, offered only as scaffolding to be kept, corrected, or thrown away as the real story surfaces.

I will write the next page the same way: beginning with the confirmed, leaving the unknown visibly open, and letting Aunt's real presence return to the page only as much as memory actually allows.

sections.body:
The one thing I know is this: Sunday meant pancakes, and pancakes meant Aunt.

I start there because it is the only ground I can stand on without guessing. Aunt, in her kitchen — I cannot tell you which kitchen, or which year, or whether the windows looked onto a street or a garden. I do not remember what she wore, or whether she hummed, or whether she spoke at all. I do not remember if anyone else was there. Those are blanks, and I am leaving them blank.

What I have is the fact of her, and the fact of pancakes, and a word I can only call ritual. Sunday came, and Aunt made them. That is the whole of it. No smell, no colour, no sound — I will not dress the scene in details that belong to someone else's memory and call them mine.

The rest of this story will have to be built the way a life is actually recovered: slowly, and only where the record holds. I begin with the one thing I am sure of. Aunt. Sunday. Pancakes.

That is enough to start.
